clue.text: Doctor is here to speculate on  …

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters that follow are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A medic turns up at a talk, ready to hold forth on whatever the next clue brings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' looks like a link word but is part of the letters to rearrange. The ellipsis runs this clue into 2 Down; 'on' is only the bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: To theorise is to form ideas without proof, which is what speculating means: a straight synonym.

clue.text: …  those kitted out for the bench

definitions.text: those kitted out for the bench

blocks.clueFragment: those kitted out for the bench
blocks.note: surface reading: carpenters or workers dressed for the workbench
setter's reading: the bench at a football ground, where replacement players sit in their kit

explanation.surface: Following on from 1 Down, someone ponders the workers dressed for their workbench.
explanation.walkthrough: A bench suggests a judge's seat or a workshop, but here it is the touchline bench where replacement players wait.
explanation.definitionFit: Substitutes in team sports wait in full kit on the bench, ready to come on; the short form is the plural abbreviation.

clue.text: Angry Central American group provides material reinforcement

indicators.note: central asks only for the letter at the very middle of the word it describes

blocks.note: the middle of a five-letter word
US is a common abbreviation for American
a set is a group

explanation.surface: A furious band from Central America supplies extra fabric for strengthening something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central American' reads as one region, but 'Central' belongs with 'Angry' and 'American' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A gusset is a piece of cloth sewn into a garment to strengthen or enlarge it, so it is literally reinforcement made of material.

clue.text: Too controlled to be a nonentity

blocks.note: too in the sense of as well
to run a business is to control it

explanation.surface: Someone so restrained that they fade into insignificance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too controlled' reads as excessively restrained; split it into two separate synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a horse or person who finishes out of the places, hence an undistinguished, unimportant figure.

clue.text: Drunk, pacing around all morning, becomes offensive

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so the word next to it is jumbled
around means the jumbled letters go on either side of the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written, then jumbled
AM covers the whole of the morning, before noon

explanation.surface: A drinker spends the whole morning pacing up and down and turns aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' looks like an adjective for rude behaviour, but it is the military noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An offensive is an organised attack or series of operations, the same as a military campaign.

clue.text: Do they love all the words in this clue?

definitions.text: Do they love all the words in this clue?

blocks.clueFragment: Do they love all the words in this clue?
blocks.note: surface reading: a question about whether someone is fond of this particular clue
setter's reading: people who love words in general, from the Greek for word and lover

explanation.walkthrough: The question seems to be about the clue itself; it really describes people who adore words of every kind.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek roots mean word plus lover, so these are people who delight in vocabulary and language.

clue.text: Manipulate Western opinion

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for western
an angle is a point of view

explanation.surface: A call to spin the views held in the West.
explanation.definitionFit: To wangle is to obtain or arrange something by trickery or persuasion, which is a kind of manipulating.

clue.text: You can't order it in a strange pub

definitions.text: You can't order it in a strange pub

blocks.clueFragment: You can't order it in a strange pub
blocks.note: surface reading: some drink that a particular unfamiliar pub does not serve
setter's reading: in a pub where nobody knows you, the bar staff cannot know your regular drink

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like a missing item on the menu; the point is that a regular's shorthand order only works where you are known.
explanation.definitionFit: Regulars ask for their customary drink with this phrase, relying on the barman remembering it.

clue.text: Dull specialist clothing

blocks.note: first meaning: a boring person obsessed with a narrow hobby
second meaning: a hooded waterproof jacket

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang an anorak is a nerdy enthusiast, after the jackets worn by trainspotters.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a waterproof hooded jacket and, by association, an obsessive, unexciting hobbyist.

clue.text: Joined by kids wanting to see a picture

definitions.text: Joined by kids wanting to see a picture

blocks.clueFragment: Joined by kids wanting to see a picture
blocks.note: surface reading: children teaming up to go to the cinema
setter's reading: the numbered marks in a puzzle book that children connect with lines to reveal a drawing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Picture' suggests a film outing; really it is the children's puzzle where lines between numbered points make an image.
explanation.definitionFit: In a join-the-dots puzzle children draw lines between numbered marks until a picture appears.

clue.text: Show up long defective clearing mechanism

indicators.note: something defective is faulty or broken, so the preceding words are out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A faulty device for clearing something takes a long time to appear.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowplough is a vehicle or blade that clears snow from roads, a machine for clearing.

clue.text: Comedy slam? How fashionable!

blocks.note: wit is humour
to slam is to strike hard

explanation.surface: A cutting stand-up insult greeted with mock admiration for being so trendy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slam' looks like a put-down that follows the comedy; it is just a verb for striking.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'with it' is colloquial for being up to date and stylish, an idiom for trendy.

clue.text: Food critics have had more of them than you

definitions.text: Food critics have had more of them than you

blocks.clueFragment: Food critics have had more of them than you
blocks.note: surface reading: restaurant reviewers simply eat out more often than ordinary people

blocks.clueFragment: had more of them than you
blocks.note: setter's reading: the idiom 'I've had more ... than you've had', boasting of greater experience

explanation.walkthrough: The British boast 'I've had more of these than you've had' claims long experience; food critics fit it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooked midday or evening meals served warm; the boasting idiom uses them as a measure of years lived.

clue.text: Got off with a thin English duke

blocks.note: taken as written
light as in light, thin fabric
E is the abbreviation for English
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: Someone made a conquest of a skinny English aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got off with' is British slang for a romantic encounter, but 'with' only joins the parts here.
explanation.definitionFit: To alight is to step down from a bus or train, so having alighted is having disembarked.

clue.text: Keep at deregulator to hold back bureaucracy

indicators.note: the words before this phrase hold the letters wanted, inside them
back tells the solver to read the held letters from right to left

blocks.note: the run from the end of the first word to the start of the third

explanation.surface: Keep a government deregulator around to restrain officialdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape is the excessive paperwork and rules of officialdom, named after the ribbon once used on documents.

clue.text: Identify standard measure of accuracy

blocks.note: first meaning: to locate exactly
second meaning: the tiny spot used to describe perfect precision

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning comes from the phrase 'pinpoint accuracy', where the word sets the standard for precision.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to find or name precisely; as a noun it is the minute point by which precision is judged.

clue.text: Any envelope for a record correspondence?

indicators.note: an envelope wraps around its contents, so the first word encloses what follows

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: Asking whether some envelope will do for posting a vinyl disc by mail.
explanation.walkthrough: Envelope and correspondence suggest letters in the post; correspondence here means similarity.
explanation.definitionFit: An analogy is a likeness or parallel between two things, and correspondence in that sense means similarity.

clue.text: Its rare to find good evidence of poor housekeeping

definitions.note: the phrase describes the answer, a noun for something scarce

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
old dust lying about shows the cleaning has been neglected

explanation.surface: It is unusual to come across proper proof that someone keeps a slovenly house.
explanation.definitionFit: Something scarce and highly prized is said to be 'like gold dust', so the phrase stands for rarity.

clue.text: Bend you can't take at a clip!

definitions.text: Bend you can't take at a clip!

blocks.clueFragment: Bend you can't take at a clip!
blocks.note: surface reading: a sharp curve in the road too tight to drive round at speed
setter's reading: a clip is also a grip for holding hair in place

explanation.walkthrough: At a clip means at speed, and a very tight road bend is named after a hair clip, so both senses fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A very sharp U-shaped road bend is named after the U-shaped wire used to fasten hair.

clue.text: Criminal had a nice estate in Spain

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so the following letters are bent out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A crook on the run enjoyed a lovely property on the Spanish coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacienda is a large landed estate or ranch with a main house in Spain or Spanish America.

clue.text: No interest in a walk by close

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used

blocks.note: taken as written
a path is a walk or footway
the end of this short word

explanation.surface: Someone has no enthusiasm for a stroll nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By close' looks like 'nearby'; 'close' really points to the end of 'by'.
explanation.definitionFit: Apathy is a lack of interest, enthusiasm or concern, so a plain synonym for indifference.

clue.text: Keep half of cake star left

indicators.note: half of asks for just the front portion of each of the following words

blocks.note: the front half of a four-letter word
the front half of a four-letter word
the front half of a four-letter word

explanation.surface: Instruction to save half the cake and leave it for the star of the show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half of' applies to all three words, not just 'cake'.
explanation.definitionFit: A keep is the strongest central tower of a medieval fortress, so it names part or the whole of a fortified building.

clue.text: Shoddy lot stocked by company

indicators.note: stocked by means held as stock inside the firm, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company
a heap is a lot, as in heaps of time

explanation.surface: A batch of poor-quality goods sold by a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapo is informal for cheap and of poor quality, matching shoddy as an adjective.

clue.text: Principal meal, picked up on tray

blocks.note: first meaning: the chief dish of a dinner
second meaning: what you collect on your tray at a canteen counter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' tempts a sound-alike reading, but nothing here is spoken; it is just the canteen dish you collect.
explanation.definitionFit: The most substantial dish of a meal, between starter and dessert, is the one a diner carries off on a tray.

clue.text: It originally died out twice

indicators.note: originally points to the start of each word, so only initials are taken

blocks.note: the initials of the two words
the same pair repeated

explanation.surface: A note on some creature whose kind vanished from the earth not once but twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: this bird famously became extinct, giving the phrase 'dead as a dodo'.
explanation.definitionFit: The dodo was a flightless Mauritian bird wiped out in the seventeenth century, the classic example of extinction.

clue.text: Stride endlessly over ground

indicators.note: without its ends means losing both the first and last letters
in a down clue, over means turned the other way up

blocks.note: the word with its outside letters dropped

explanation.surface: A walker marches tirelessly across the terrain.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground and dirt both mean soil or earth, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Quiet! Nora's backed another girl

indicators.note: backed means the name is read from back to front

blocks.note: sh is the call for silence
taken as written

explanation.surface: Hush now: Nora has thrown her support behind a different girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharon is a female given name, so another girl's name besides Nora.

clue.text: Must ripe bananas become the least wholesome?

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Do bananas have to be overripe to count as the unhealthiest fruit?
explanation.definitionFit: Impurest is the superlative of impure, meaning most contaminated, the opposite of most wholesome.
